abstract: Benchmark results tell clinics which gene-prioritization system to trust and the field what counts as progress. Standard benchmarking practice --- testing each system using its latest knowledge databases --- can inflate system accuracy estimates and invite data leakage. We formalize the Fairbench protocol: testing may use only knowledge available strictly before the patient's assessment. Against prepublication snapshots dated by case report, on one public case collection, standard benchmarking inflated Top-1 accuracy by 40.5--80.5 percentage points across Exomiser, LIRICAL, Phrank and Phen2Disease. In every system, over half the tested patients had a causal-gene phenotype association whose only recorded source was their case publication. Reassessing three systems' published benchmarks with reproduced or reconstructed references showed the same direction in all five comparisons. Retesting undiagnosed patients with the latest knowledge database is good care. But benchmark results are read as performance at the patient's assessment, and Fairbench is a necessary data-hygiene condition for that reading.
